title: NASA-ISRO NISAR Satellite Captures Stunning Antarctic Landscape in New Radar Data
excerpt: The joint India-U.S. satellite's synthetic aperture radar has revealed a hummingbird-shaped terrain formation in Antarctica, showcasing the mission's unprecedented ability to map the frozen continent.
body:
• NISAR satellite, launched in July 2025, has captured radar images revealing a hummingbird-shaped terrain in Antarctica.
  • Since entering its full science phase in February 2026, NISAR has produced over 100,000 data products to enhance understanding of ice sheet changes and sea level rise.
  • The $1.5 billion mission is a collaboration between NASA and ISRO, making it the most expensive Earth-imaging satellite ever built.
  • NISAR's data is freely accessible, supporting global research in climate science and disaster response.
Key Takeaways
  • NISAR satellite reveals a hummingbird-shaped terrain in Antarctica through advanced radar imaging.
  • Launched in July 2025, NISAR has produced over 100,000 data products since February 2026.
  • The $1.5 billion mission enhances understanding of ice sheet changes and sea level rise.
  • NISAR's data is freely accessible, supporting global research in climate science and disaster response.

A Bird's-Eye View of the Ice

The NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar satellite, known as NISAR, has captured a radar image of an Antarctic landscape formation that bears a striking resemblance to a hummingbird, according to India New England News. The image is part of a growing body of data from the joint U.S.-India satellite, which entered its full science phase in 2026 after launching from ISRO's Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota on July 30, 2025.

The finding underscores the remarkable detail that NISAR's dual-frequency radar can extract from beneath clouds, darkness, and even snow cover — conditions that have long limited satellite observation of Earth's most remote continent.

The Most Advanced Radar in Orbit

NISAR is the most expensive Earth-imaging satellite ever built, with NASA contributing approximately $1.2 billion and ISRO around $90 million, according to AFP. The spacecraft carries two synthetic aperture radar instruments operating at different wavelengths — an L-band system (24-centimeter wavelength) built by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and an S-band system (10-centimeter wavelength) provided by ISRO's Space Applications Centre.

"The unique feature, from my perspective, is the degree of comprehensiveness of the coverage in space and time."

— Paul Rosen, NISAR Project Scientist, NASA JPL

The satellite orbits at 747 kilometers altitude and scans nearly all of Earth's land and ice surfaces twice every 12 days. Its 12-meter deployable mesh antenna reflector — the largest radar antenna reflector NASA has ever sent into space — can detect vertical and horizontal ground shifts of less than one centimeter, according to Science magazine.

Unprecedented Antarctic Coverage

NISAR's orbital configuration gives it access to Antarctica's deep interior, close to the South Pole — a region that other large imaging radar satellites have struggled to reach, according to NASA. This coverage is critical because Antarctica's ice sheets hold 90% of the world's glacier ice. If they were to melt entirely, global sea levels would rise by roughly 60 meters.

"Our planet has the thermostat set on high, and Earth's ice is responding by speeding up its motion and melting faster," said Alex Gardner, a glaciologist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. "We need to better understand the processes at play, and NISAR will provide measurements to do that."

The satellite's L-band radar can penetrate through snow to track ice motion underneath, while its S-band radar is sensitive to snow moisture, which indicates melting. Both signals can see through clouds and polar darkness, enabling year-round monitoring during Antarctica's months-long winter nights.

Data Deluge for Global Science

In late February 2026, NISAR released over 100,000 Level 1 to Level 3 L-band data products through the Alaska Satellite Facility, according to NASA. By the end of its planned three-year mission, the spacecraft is expected to generate up to 140 petabytes of data — roughly equivalent to NASA's entire existing Earth science archive, according to Science magazine.

Ian Joughin, a glaciologist at the University of Washington and NISAR's cryosphere lead, told NASA that the satellite would deliver "a consistent time-lapse movie" of ice motion, helping scientists understand how and why changes are occurring and predict future patterns.

The mission also marks a milestone in U.S.-India space relations. NISAR is the first hardware collaboration between NASA and ISRO on an Earth-observing mission, building on earlier cooperation including the 2008 Chandrayaan-1 lunar mission. Hardware was built on separate continents and integrated at ISRO's Satellite Integration and Testing Establishment in Bengaluru before launch.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad, NISAR represents a high-profile example of India's growing role in cutting-edge global science. ISRO provided the spacecraft bus, the S-band radar, the GSLV launch vehicle, and launch services. Indian scientists including Deepak Putrevu, co-lead of the ISRO science team at the Space Applications Centre in Ahmedabad, and Sushil Kumar Singh, an ISRO glaciologist, are central to the mission's research.

The satellite's data is freely and openly available to researchers worldwide, meaning Indian universities and institutions can access the same high-resolution radar imagery as their American counterparts — an equal footing that reflects the mission's 50-50 partnership structure.

What's Next

NISAR's science phase will continue through at least 2028, with the satellite producing increasingly detailed maps of Earth's changing surfaces. Paul Rosen presented early findings at the ASCEND 2026 conference in May, covering initial imagery and the science pipeline for disaster response, agriculture, and climate monitoring. The mission's Antarctic data, including formations like the hummingbird landscape, will feed into improved models of ice sheet behavior and more accurate sea level rise projections — information with direct implications for coastal communities worldwide.
